chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Al-Fadl ibn Shadhan and Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, all together from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskam, from Al-Halbi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
When the fasting one vomits, then upon him is the making up of that day, and if nausea comes to him without him vomiting, then let him complete his fast.

key_terms.ذَرَعَهُ: nausea came to him / he felt nauseous

ai.seo_question: Does vomiting break the fast in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of distinguishing between involuntary and voluntary acts in breaking the fast, a key nuance in Shia fiqh. It clarifies that mere nausea or the urge to vomit does not invalidate the fast, ensuring that the believer is not penalized for natural bodily sensations unless the act of regurgitation actually occurs. This ruling reflects the Shia emphasis on ease and the removal of hardship (raf' al-haraj) in religious obligations.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Ismail, from Al Fazl Bin ShAzan and Abu Ali Al Ashary, from Muhammad Bin Abdul Jabbar, altogether from Safwan Bin Yahya, from Ibn Muskam, from Al Halby, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘When the Fasting one vomits, so upon him would be the making up for that day, and if he nauseates from without vomiting, so let him complete his Fast’.
en.sarwar: 1. Muhammad ibn ‘Isma‘il has narrated from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from and Abu Ali al-Ash’ariy from Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Jabbar all from Safwan ibn Yahya from ibn Muskan from al-Halabiy who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘
If one fasting vomits, one is required to make Qada’ (compensatory fast for) that day; and if one feels nausea but does not vomit, one must complete the fast.’”
